newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - U.S. dealers divided, cautious about FOMC.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - U.S. dealers divided, cautious about FOMC.

text.p: The Wall Street community is sharply divided about the outcome of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on Tuesday, with a slight majority leaning toward unchanged policy, according to a Reuters poll.
As a result of the uncertainty about the U.S. interest rate outlook, dealers said Wall Street firms are reluctant to set up large positions ahead of the central bank's decision.
Market volatility is, therefore, to be expected following the Federal Reserve's announcement which should come at around 1415 EDT/1815 GMT on Tuesday, dealers added.
In a Reuters survey of the 39 U.S. primary dealers:
-- 21 expected the Fed to keep interest rates unchanged,

-- 18 forecast a 25-basis-points hike in the 5.50-percent federal funds rate -- including three who expected an increase in the 5.00-percent discount rate as well. Two of these firms predicted the Fed Board would raise the discount rate to 5.25 percent and one to 5.50 percent.
The Fed Board last moved on the discount rate in January 1996, lowering it by 25 points amid signs of a weak economy.
The Fed resumed tightening credit on March 25, raising the funds rate by 25 points as anti-inflation insurance.

Devlin, whose firm's forecast was based on the absence of an "hawkish" anti-inflation stance in Greenspan's speech, said it was difficult for anyone to set up large positions in the absence of a clear-cut case for Fed policy.

"I don't know if anyone is making any big bets. There is no one out there who made any huge bet because the (Treasury yield) curve is basically unchanged from where it was for the last two weeks," Devlin pointed out. "The (Treasury) market probably is at a stand-off here."
Devlin also said it was difficult to predict how markets would react to a Fed decision -- or the lack thereof.
"If the Fed does not move, the curve will steepen. If the Fed tightens, the market can go any which way," Devlin added.
Two lines of reasoning are essentially accounting for the division of opinions on Wall Street.
Those expecting a steady policy cite:
-- still low inflation, expected slowdown, lack of support for a rate hike, the impact of the balanced-budget deal.
Those expecting a rate hike cite:
-- the Fed's emphasis on a preemptive policy to address inflationary risks before inflation emerges, resulting in higher interest rates threatening to bring about a downturn.
Chief market strategist Matthew Alexy at CS First Boston expected the Fed to keep interest rates unchanged as "the Fed is in the process of rebalancing interest rates."

"The Fed is still trying to understand how fast the economy can grow without generating inflation," Alexy said. "They want to space out their movements and respond that way instead of moving very quickly."
Alexy agreed the strong U.S. economy does not require major policy changes -- just "a rebalance in policy."
"It's a mirror image of 1995," Alexy said, in reference to the small easing moves the Fed took in July and December 1995.
